mainTopic: Which languages holy books may be written in, and why Greek is allowed for a ספר תורה (the story of תלמי המלך).
overview: The גמרא is working on a contradiction. Our משנה says holy books may be written in any language, but a ברייתא says a verse written in translation is not holy, and a scroll only counts if it is written in אשורית. רבא first answers that the משנה means a foreign language written in Hebrew letters, but אביי knocks this down. The next two answers also fall. The first says the sources follow different תנאים, but that fails because רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows Greek. The second says the ברייתא is about תפילין and מזוזות, which must stay 'as they are' because of 'והיו', but it fails because they contain no Aramaic. The גמרא then says the ברייתא is about the מגילה, which must be written 'ככתבם וכלשונם', and it does have Aramaic words like 'פתגם' and 'יקר'. רב אשי gives another answer: the ברייתא is about the other books of תנ״ך and follows רבי יהודה, who allowed Greek only for a ספר תורה. The amud ends with the reason Greek was allowed: the story of תלמי המלך, whose seventy-two separated זקנים all made the same changes in their translations.

steps.title: Our letters versus their letters
steps.stepSummary: רבא resolves the contradiction: the משנה allows another language written in Hebrew letters, while the ברייתא rejects a text written in foreign letters.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here (the משנה) is speaking about our script; there (the ברייתא) is speaking about their script.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא. It splits them into two different cases based on which alphabet is used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says ספרים may be written in any language. The ברייתא says they must be in אשורית. According to this answer, the language may be foreign as long as the letters are Hebrew letters (the משנה), but foreign letters make the scroll not holy (the ברייתא).

keyTerms.meaning: Here, in this source (used to contrast two sources)
Script, the form of the letters

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up language and script. 'Our script' here means Hebrew letters, even when the words themselves are in another language.

phrases.english: Here, it is in our script,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the משנה: the words are foreign, but they're written with Hebrew letters.

phrases.english: there, it is in their script.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּאן בְּגּוֹפָן שֶׁלָּנוּ, כָּאן בְּגּוֹפָן שֶׁלָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא that was raised on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two sources are talking about different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא seem to clash about which languages are allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a foreign language in Hebrew letters; the ברייתא is about foreign letters.

steps.title: אביי: then why mention translation at all?
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that if the ברייתא were about foreign letters, it would not need to talk about Hebrew changed into Aramaic. Even Hebrew left as Hebrew would be invalid in foreign letters.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: How did you explain that ברייתא? As speaking about their script? If so, why does it specifically mention Hebrew Bible text written as Aramaic translation, and Aramaic translation written as Hebrew Bible text? Even Bible text written as Bible text, and translation written as translation, would also be invalid, because it teaches: unless one writes it in אשורית, on a scroll, in ink!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's answer. He shows that the cases the ברייתא chooses don't fit the explanation that it is about foreign letters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא's problem were foreign letters, then switching languages would be beside the point. Even an untranslated Hebrew text in foreign letters would fail, since the ברייתא ends by requiring אשורית. The fact that the ברייתא focuses on translation shows that it is talking about language, not script.

keyTerms.meaning: You established, you explained (a source as speaking about a certain case)
Bible text in its original Hebrew
The square Hebrew script used for a ספר תורה

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is רבא, who gave the answer in Step 1.

phrases.english: How did you explain that one?
phrases.notes: "That one" is the ברייתא.

phrases.english: As referring to their script?
Why specifically Bible text that one wrote as translation
and translation that one wrote as Bible text?
Even Bible text written as Bible text
and translation written as translation would also be invalid.
For it teaches:

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיִּכְתְּבֶנּוּ אַשּׁוּרִית עַל הַסֵּפֶר בִּדְיוֹ!
phrases.english: Not until one writes it in Ashurit, on a scroll, in ink!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: בְּמַאי אוֹקֵימְתָּא לְהַהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer from Step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that the ברייתא is about foreign letters (גופן שלהן).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If foreign letters were the problem, the ברייתא's focus on translation would be pointless. Even untranslated text in foreign letters would fail, since the ברייתא requires אשורית anyway.

steps.title: A new answer: the רבנן versus רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops רבא's answer and says the two sources reflect a מחלוקת: the משנה follows the רבנן, and the ברייתא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is not difficult: this one follows the רבנן, and that one follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on the first answer and offers a new one. It says the משנה and the ברייתא simply follow different תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן allow ספרים to be written in any language, which matches the משנה. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל is stricter about other languages, so the ברייתא's requirement of אשורית is credited to him.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

phrases.english: Rather, it is not difficult:
this one follows the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: "This one" is our משנה, which allows any language.

phrases.english: that one follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
phrases.notes: "That one" is the ברייתא, which requires אשורית.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא רַבָּנַן, הָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבא's answer, which אביי knocked down in Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning each source to a different תנא (תנאי היא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources were assumed to reflect one shared view.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה follows the רבנן, and the ברייתא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: But רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows Greek
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second answer: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל also allows Greek, so he can't be the source of a ברייתא that requires only אשורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, there is also Greek!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second answer. It shows that the ברייתא does not match רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's actual opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that ספרים may be written in Greek as well. The ברייתא, however, says nothing besides אשורית works. So the ברייתא can't follow his view.

phrases.english: If it follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
there is also Greek!
phrases.notes: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows ספרים in Greek too, but the ברייתא says only אשורית.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הָא אִיכָּא יְוָנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows Greek, yet the ברייתא allows only אשורית. The two opinions don't match.

steps.title: Scrolls versus תפילין and מזוזות
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: the משנה is about ספרים, which may be written in other languages, while the ברייתא is about תפילין and מזוזות, which must be written in אשורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is not difficult: here it refers to books, there it refers to תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer. It splits the sources by the type of object being written. This answer is examined and then dropped in Steps 6–9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ordinary ספרים, other languages are acceptable, as the משנה teaches. תפילין and מזוזות have a stricter rule: only אשורית, on parchment, in ink. The ברייתא's strict requirement applies to them.
steps.whyThisMatters: The reason given for this answer, 'והיו' (Step 7), stays valid even after the answer itself is dropped. The גמרא uses it again in Step 15.

phrases.english: Rather, it is not difficult:
here, it refers to books,
phrases.notes: This is the משנה: scrolls of Tanach may be written in other languages.

phrases.english: there, it refers to tefillin and mezuzot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בִּסְפָרִים, כָּאן בִּתְפִלִּין וּמְזוּזוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer from Step 3, which was knocked down in Step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by type of object (אוקימתא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was thought to be about ספרים, like the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about תפילין and מזוזות, which require אשורית; the משנה is about ספרים.

steps.title: Why must תפילין and מזוזות be written in אשורית?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that תפילין and מזוזות must be written only in אשורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason for the rule about תפילין and מזוזות?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just said that תפילין and מזוזות must be written in אשורית. Now it asks why. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last answer split the cases: ספרים may be written in any language, but תפילין and מזוזות may not. A split like that needs a reason. The גמרא asks what makes תפילין and מזוזות different.

keyTerms.meaning: Boxes with parchments of פסוקים, worn on the arm and head
Parchments with פסוקים, fixed on doorposts

phrases.english: Tefillin and mezuzot, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the distinction made in Step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that תפילין and מזוזות must be written only in אשורית.

steps.title: The word 'והיו' means they must stay as they are
steps.stepSummary: The Torah writes 'והיו' about them, which teaches that they must remain in their original form.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written about them, 'And they shall be.' This means they must stay exactly as they are.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The word 'והיו' teaches that תפילין and מזוזות must be written exactly as the Torah wrote them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'והיו' comes from the root 'to be.' The גמרא reads it as 'they must be the way they are.' So no change of language or script is allowed for תפילין and מזוזות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And they shall be,' a word in the פסוק about תפילין and מזוזות
They must stay in their original form

phrases.english: Because it is written about them: "And they shall be"
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק in דברים about 'these words' being on your heart, which leads into תפילין and מזוזה.

phrases.english: they must be as they are.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'והיו' means 'as they are,' so תפילין and מזוזות may not be changed into another language or script.

steps.title: There is no Aramaic in תפילין and מזוזות
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא spoke of Aramaic written as Hebrew. But תפילין and מזוזות contain no Aramaic, unlike the Torah, which has 'יגר שהדותא'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what Aramaic written as Hebrew could there be? In the Torah, fine, there is 'יגר שהדותא.' But here, what Aramaic is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. The ברייתא talked about Aramaic that someone wrote in Hebrew. That case cannot happen in תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's wording assumes the text has some Aramaic in it to begin with. The Torah does have Aramaic words, like 'יגר שהדותא' in בראשית. The פסוקים of תפילין and מזוזות have no Aramaic at all, so the ברייתא cannot be about them.

keyTerms.meaning: An Aramaic passage that someone wrote in Hebrew
It makes sense for this case (but not the other)
'Mound of witness,' Aramaic words in the Torah (בראשית ל״א)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about the rule for תפילין. It is about the ברייתא's wording: an Aramaic piece written in Hebrew. That case cannot exist in תפילין and מזוזות.

phrases.english: What Aramaic that one wrote as Hebrew is there?
Granted, in the Torah there is "Yegar sahaduta,"
phrases.notes: That is what לבן called the pile of stones, in Aramaic, when he made a deal with יעקב.

phrases.english: but here, what Aramaic is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 5, that the ברייתא is about תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is talking about תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's case needs Aramaic in the text, and תפילין and מזוזות contain none.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about מגילה, the משנה is about ספרים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops תפילין and מזוזות and says the ברייתא is about מגילת אסתר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is not hard: here it is about the מגילה, there it is about ספרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. The strict ברייתא is about the מגילה. The lenient משנה is about other ספרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אלא' shows that the תפילין answer is being dropped. Now the strict rule moves to מגילת אסתר. The גמרא will next give a reason and check whether the מגילה has any Aramaic.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the sources speak about different cases

phrases.english: Rather, it is not difficult:
here, regarding the Megilla; there, regarding books.
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the strict ברייתא and 'there' is the lenient משנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בִּמְגִילָּה, כָּאן בִּסְפָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer that Step 8 knocked down.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was about תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about מגילת אסתר, and the משנה is about ספרים.

steps.title: Why is the מגילה strict?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason the מגילה must be written in its original language.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason for the מגילה?
steps.whatsHappening: Just as it did for תפילין, the גמרא asks for the source of the מגילה's strict rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A strict rule for one book needs its own reason. Without one, the מגילה would follow the regular rule for ספרים.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason for the מגילה's rule?

phrases.english: The Megilla, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the answer in Step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the מגילה's strict writing rule.

steps.title: 'ככתבם וכלשונם' means as written and in its language
steps.stepSummary: The מגילה itself says 'ככתבם וכלשונם,' so it must stay in its own script and language.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written in it: 'According to their writing and according to their language.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from a פסוק in the מגילה. The phrase 'ככתבם וכלשונם' teaches that the מגילה must keep its original script and language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ככתבם' means its script, and 'וכלשונם' means its language. So both changes are ruled out for the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: According to their writing and their language (אסתר ח׳:ט׳)

phrases.english: since it is written in it: "According to their writing and according to their language."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'ככתבם וכלשונם' requires the מגילה to stay in its original script and language.

steps.title: Is there any Aramaic in the מגילה?
steps.stepSummary: The same problem comes back: the ברייתא needs Aramaic written as Hebrew, and the מגילה seems to be all Hebrew.
steps.simpleTranslation: What Aramaic written as Hebrew is there in the מגילה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the same challenge it used against תפילין. Where is there any Aramaic in the מגילה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the exact words of Step 8, now aimed at the new answer. If the מגילה has no Aramaic, the ברייתא's case cannot be about it either.

phrases.english: What Aramaic that one wrote as Hebrew is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the challenge of Step 8, now against the מגילה answer of Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is about the מגילה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's case needs Aramaic in the text, and the מגילה appears to be all Hebrew.

steps.title: Aramaic words in the מגילה: 'פתגם' and 'יקר'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא points to 'פתגם', and רב נחמן בר יצחק points to 'יקר'. Both are Aramaic words found in the מגילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: 'And the king's decree (פתגם) shall be heard.' רב נחמן בר יצחק said: 'And all the wives shall give honor (יקר) to their husbands.'
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the challenge. Each shows an Aramaic word inside the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each one picks a different word from the same פסוק. 'פתגם' (decree) and 'יקר' (honor) are Aramaic words, so the מגילה does have some Aramaic. That means the ברייתא's case can happen in the מגילה, and the answer of Step 9 stands.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: "And the king's decree [pitgam] shall be heard."
phrases.notes: The point is the word 'פתגם', which is Aramaic. Both quotes come from the same פסוק in אסתר א׳.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
"And all the wives shall give honor [yekar] to their husbands."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12 and saves the answer of Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual answer: shows the missing case does exist
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The מגילה is entirely in Hebrew.
steps.terutzMaskana: The מגילה contains Aramaic words such as פתגם and יקר.

steps.title: רב אשי: the ברייתא is about the other ספרים and follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer: the strict ברייתא is about the other books of תנ״ך, and it follows רבי יהודה. A supporting ברייתא is quoted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: That ברייתא is about the other books, and it follows רבי יהודה. As it was taught: תפילין and מזוזות may be written only in אשורית, and our Rabbis permitted Greek.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a whole new way to settle the clash. He says the strict ברייתא is about the rest of the books of תנ״ך, and that it follows רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the conflict is solved in two ways. The two sources speak about different books, and the strict one follows a specific תנא, רבי יהודה. A ברייתא is quoted as the source for his view: תפילין and מזוזות only in אשורית, while 'our Rabbis' allowed Greek.

keyTerms.meaning: The other books of תנ״ך (other than the Torah)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers here. First: the strict ברייתא is about the מגילה ('ככתבם וכלשונם'), which does have Aramaic words. Second, רב אשי: it is about the other ספרים of תנ״ך, following רבי יהודה.
steps.confusionAlert: The quoted ברייתא seems to say Greek is allowed even for תפילין and מזוזות. That sounds strange after 'והיו.' The גמרא itself questions this wording in Step 15.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
when that was taught, it was about the other books,
phrases.notes: 'That' is the strict ברייתא we have been trying to place all along.

phrases.english: and it follows Rabbi Yehuda.
As it was taught: tefillin and mezuzot
are written only in Ashurit,
and our Rabbis permitted Greek.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא בִּשְׁאָר סְפָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from the מגילה answer of Steps 9–13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different subject combined with assigning the source to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The strict ברייתא was about תפילין and מזוזות, or about the מגילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The strict ברייתא is about the other books of תנ״ך and follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It opens a new line that ties the rule about other languages to a specific תנא's view. The גמרא goes on to examine that view.

steps.title: Challenge: Greek cannot be allowed for תפילין and מזוזות
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא from Step 14 seemed to allow Greek for תפילין and מזוזות. The גמרא objects using the פסוק 'והיו', which means they must stay as written.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the פסוק says 'And [these words] shall be'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא that רב אשי quoted. That ברייתא said our Rabbis allowed Greek for תפילין and מזוזות, and a פסוק seems to forbid that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'והיו' teaches that the words of תפילין and מזוזות must stay exactly as they are, in their original form. So no Rabbis could have allowed them in Greek, and the ברייתא as quoted cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? It opens a challenge from a פסוק.
'And they shall be', meaning the words must stay as they are.
תפילין and מזוזות, the subject of the ברייתא being challenged.

phrases.english: But isn't it written: 'And [these words] shall be'!
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק about תפילין and מזוזות (דברים ו:ו). It is read as 'they must stay exactly as written.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the supporting ברייתא quoted in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The clause in the ברייתא that 'our Rabbis permitted Greek' for תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק 'והיו' requires תפילין and מזוזות to stay in their original form, so Greek cannot be allowed for them.

steps.title: First fix: the ברייתא is about books, not תפילין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא as talking about books: they may be written in any language, and our Rabbis permitted Greek.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: Books may be written in any language, and our Rabbis permitted Greek.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא's wording so that the allowance for Greek is about ספרים, not תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving the topic to ספרים gets around the 'והיו' problem, because that פסוק is only about תפילין and מזוזות. But this new wording creates a fresh problem, which the next step raises.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say. The גמרא is changing how the text should read.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
Books are written in any language,
and our Rabbis permitted Greek.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 15 by changing the subject of the ברייתא from תפילין to books.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא allowed Greek for תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about books, which may be written in any language, with Greek specifically mentioned.

steps.title: Challenge: 'permitted' suggests the first תנא forbade Greek
steps.stepSummary: The word 'permitted' implies the first opinion forbade Greek. But the first opinion just said any language is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They permitted'?! That implies the first תנא forbids it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds a problem with the new wording from Step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You only say someone 'permitted' something if someone else forbade it. But the first תנא already allowed every language, Greek included, so the word 'permitted' makes no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication; from this we can infer.
The first תנא, the opening opinion in a ברייתא or משנה.

phrases.english: They permitted?!
By implication, the first tanna forbids!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording proposed in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'our Rabbis permitted Greek' in the reworded ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'permitted' implies an earlier ban, but the first תנא allowed all languages, so the two clauses do not fit together.

steps.title: Second fix: our Rabbis allowed only Greek
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא again: our Rabbis allowed books to be written only in Greek, besides Hebrew.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: Our Rabbis permitted them to be written only in Greek.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes the ברייתא's wording once more. Now it reads as a limit: the only other language allowed is Greek.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Rabbis' clause no longer adds an allowance on top of the first תנא. It now disagrees with him. The first תנא allows any language, while our Rabbis allow only Greek, so 'permitted' now makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: They permitted only; this wording sets a limit.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
Our Rabbis did not permit them to be written
except in Greek.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא: רַבּוֹתֵינוּ לֹא הִתִּירוּ שֶׁיִּכָּתְבוּ אֶלָּא יְוָנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17 by turning the Rabbis' clause into a limit instead of an extra allowance.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Rabbis' clause added Greek on top of 'any language'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Rabbis disagree with the first תנא and allow only Greek besides Hebrew.
steps.whatToRemember: Final reading of the ברייתא: the first תנא says books may be written in any language, and our Rabbis say books may be written only in Hebrew or Greek.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: Greek only for a ספר תורה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה: even where Greek was allowed, it was only for a ספר תורה. This supports רב אשי's claim that the strict ברייתא follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was taught: רבי יהודה said: Even when our Rabbis permitted Greek, they permitted it only for a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing that רבי יהודה limits Greek to a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the other books of תנ״ך must stay in Hebrew. That fits רב אשי's answer in Step 14: the strict ברייתא, which requires the original language, is about the other books and follows רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: A ספר תורה, the חמשה חומשי תורה.

phrases.english: And it was taught: Rabbi Yehuda said:
Even when our Rabbis permitted Greek,
they permitted it only in a Torah scroll,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source for רבי יהודה's limited view, backing רב אשי's answer.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's claim that the strict ברייתא follows רבי יהודה and is about the other books.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי יהודה limits Greek to a ספר תורה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains how Greek can be allowed while the other books, including the מגילה, still must stay in their original language.

steps.title: The story of תלמי המלך and the seventy-two זקנים
steps.stepSummary: Greek was allowed for a ספר תורה because of תלמי המלך. He put seventy-two זקנים in separate houses and told each to write the תורה for him, and they all agreed on one way.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was because of the incident of King תלמי, as it was taught: King תלמי gathered seventy-two זקנים and put them in seventy-two separate houses, without telling them why. He went in to each one and said: Write for me the Torah of משה your teacher. הקדוש ברוך הוא gave each one wisdom, and they all agreed on one understanding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for רבי יהודה's rule by telling the story of תלמי המלך. This step sets up the scene, and the next step begins listing what the זקנים actually wrote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The זקנים were kept apart and not told why, so they could not plan together. The fact that they all wrote the same translation showed it came with help from Heaven. That is why the Greek translation of the תורה gained special approval.

phrases.english: And this was because of the incident of King Ptolemy.
As it was taught:
There was an incident with King Ptolemy
who gathered seventy-two elders
and put them into seventy-two houses

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא גִּילָּה לָהֶם עַל מָה כִּינְסָן.
phrases.english: and did not reveal to them why he had gathered them.
He went in to each and every one,
and said to them:
Write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher.
phrases.notes: He wanted it written for him in Greek, as a translation.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, placed
wisdom in the heart of each and every one
and they all agreed on one understanding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רבי יהודה allowed Greek specifically for a ספר תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Greek was allowed for a ספר תורה because of the miraculous, unanimous translation done for תלמי המלך.

steps.title: The changes the זקנים made: the first examples
steps.stepSummary: The זקנים all made the same changes so that no one would misread the תורה. The first two examples are the word order of the first פסוק and the plural in 'Let us make man.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And they wrote for him: 'God created in the beginning.' 'I will make man in image and in likeness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts listing the identical changes every זקן made in his translation. The list continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each change prevents a reader from drawing a dangerous wrong idea, such as the false belief that there is more than one power. All seventy-two made the same changes without talking to each other, which is the miracle of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: In the beginning; the first word of the תורה.
I will make (singular), written instead of 'נעשה' (let us make).

steps.confusionAlert: These are not the actual words of the תורה. They are the deliberate changes the זקנים made in the Greek for תלמי, so that he would not misunderstand.

phrases.english: And they wrote for him:
'God created in the beginning.'
phrases.notes: The real פסוק says 'בראשית ברא אלהים.' They flipped the order so no one would read it as if 'בראשית' created God.

phrases.english: 'I will make man in image and in likeness.'
phrases.notes: The פסוק says 'נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו,' in plural. They wrote singular so no one would think there are many powers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by listing what the זקנים wrote.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The זקנים all made the same protective changes to the translation, showing it came with help from Heaven.

steps.title: Creation finished on the sixth day, and 'He created him'
steps.stepSummary: The זקנים wrote that ה׳ finished His work on the sixth day and rested on the seventh. They also wrote 'male and female He created him' instead of 'them.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They wrote: 'And He finished on the sixth day, and He rested on the seventh day.' They also wrote: 'Male and female He created him,' and they did not write 'He created them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list of changes from step 21 with two more examples from the Creation story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original פסוק says ה׳ finished on the seventh day, which someone could misread as ה׳ working on שבת itself. 'Created them' could seem to clash with an earlier פסוק that speaks of one person being created, so they wrote 'him.' Both changes keep the same meaning while closing off a wrong reading.

keyTerms.meaning: He created them (the original wording in the תורה)

steps.confusionAlert: These are NOT changes to our ספר תורה. They are only how the זקנים wrote the Greek translation for תלמי המלך.

phrases.english: "And He finished on the sixth day
phrases.notes: In our תורה it says ה׳ finished on the seventh day. They wrote 'sixth' instead.

phrases.english: and He rested on the seventh day."
"Male and female He created him,"
and they did not write "He created them."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of changes that began in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The זקנים wrote that ה׳ finished on the sixth day and created 'him,' so that no one would misunderstand Creation.

steps.title: 'Let Me go down' and שרה laughing among her relatives
steps.stepSummary: At the Tower of Bavel they wrote 'let Me go down' in the singular. They also wrote that שרה laughed among her relatives.
steps.simpleTranslation: They wrote: 'Come, let Me go down and confuse their language there.' And: 'And Sarah laughed among her relatives.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two more changes, one from the Tower of Bavel and one from the story of שרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original 'let us go down' is plural, which could be misread as more than one god, so they wrote it in the singular. Our תורה says שרה laughed 'inside herself.' The common explanation is that writing 'among her relatives' shows why she was criticized and אברהם was not: she laughed in front of others.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us go down (the original plural wording)

phrases.english: "Come, let Me go down
phrases.notes: Our תורה says נרדה, 'let us go down.' Here it is singular, 'Me.'

phrases.english: and confuse their language there."
"And Sarah laughed among her relatives."
phrases.notes: Our תורה says בקרבה, 'inside herself.' The two words look very similar in Hebrew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more items to the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: They wrote 'let Me go down' to avoid any idea of many gods, and 'among her relatives' for שרה's laughter.

steps.title: An ox and a trough, and משה's 'carrier of people'
steps.stepSummary: They softened יעקב's words about שמעון ולוי so the sons do not sound like murderers. They also wrote that משה put his family on a 'carrier of people' instead of a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: They wrote: 'For in their anger they killed an ox, and in their will they uprooted a trough.' And: 'And משה took his wife and his sons, and set them on a carrier of people.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lists two more changes: one from יעקב's blessings and one from משה's trip back to מצרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our תורה says שמעון ולוי 'killed a man.' The Greek version said 'an ox,' so the sons of יעקב would not look like murderers to the king. Instead of 'donkey,' which could look lowly for a great leader like משה, they wrote 'carrier of people,' which could mean a nicer animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Carrier of people (an animal that carries riders)

phrases.english: "For in their anger they killed an ox
phrases.notes: These are יעקב's words about שמעון ולוי. Our תורה says they killed a man.

phrases.english: and in their will they uprooted a trough."
phrases.notes: Our תורה says here that they maimed an ox. The Greek version moved the ox to the first half and put a trough here.

phrases.english: "And Moshe took his wife and his sons
and set them on a carrier of people."
phrases.notes: Our תורה says 'on the donkey.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list, now reaching the end of בראשית and the start of שמות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: They wrote 'ox' and 'trough' instead of 'man' and 'ox,' and 'carrier of people' instead of 'donkey.'

steps.title: Four hundred years, and the 'elect' of Israel
steps.stepSummary: They wrote that בני ישראל lived in מצרים and other lands for four hundred years. They also used the word זאטוטי, 'the elect,' in two פסוקים at הר סיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: They wrote: 'And the dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt and in other lands, was four hundred years.' And: 'And he sent the elect of the children of Israel.' And: 'And upon the elect of the children of Israel He did not lay His hand.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the last changes on this amud, all from ספר שמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read plainly, our פסוק says בני ישראל were in מצרים for 430 years, but they were not there that long. The Greek version adds 'other lands' and says 400 years, so the count is not wrong. In the two פסוקים at הר סיני, our תורה uses two different words, נערי ('youths') and אצילי ('nobles'). The Greek version used one word, זאטוטי ('the elect'), for both.

keyTerms.meaning: Youths (the original wording in the first פסוק)
Nobles (the original wording in the second פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Every item in this list follows the same pattern. The זקנים, all on their own and in separate houses, changed the wording in exactly the same way so a non-Jewish king would not misread the תורה. That miracle is why Greek got a special status for writing a ספר תורה.

phrases.english: "And the dwelling of the children of Israel
which they dwelt in Egypt
and in other lands was four hundred years."
phrases.notes: Our תורה says 430 years and mentions only מצרים. They added 'other lands' and wrote 400.

phrases.english: "And he sent the elect of the children of Israel."
phrases.notes: Our תורה says נערי, 'the youths,' the ones who brought offerings at הר סיני.

phrases.english: "And upon the elect of the children of Israel
phrases.notes: A few פסוקים later. Here our תורה says אצילי, 'the nobles.'

phrases.english: He did not lay His hand."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָשְׁבוּ בְּמִצְרָיִם וּבִשְׁאָר אֲרָצוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list, now in ספר שמות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: They wrote 'in Egypt and in other lands, four hundred years,' and used 'the elect' for both the youths and the nobles at הר סיני.
